strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem in LLM serving: obtaining speculative-decoding gains under continuous batching rather than only at batch size one.

The parameter-free design is practically appealing. Combining prompt/self-output retrieval with a fixed datastore, parallelizing retrieval on CPUs, and using tree-based verification avoids training and deploying a separate draft model.

The roofline analysis usefully explains how batch size, speculation length, and context length affect verification cost. The measured operator behavior is contrasted with the hardware-based prediction rather than presenting speedups alone.

The evaluation includes end-to-end serving measurements, batch sizes up to 64, three context-length regimes, two model/tokenizer families, and comparisons with REST and PIA. The reported gains are substantial and internally consistent with the proposed account of long-context inference.
weaknesses: The evidence does not support broad claims such as effectiveness on “any task,” dominance at “any latency requirement,” or state-of-the-art continuous-batching performance. End-to-end experiments use one customized serving stack, one Huawei accelerator, two similarly sized Llama models, and a small collection of English benchmarks. Relevant trainable and systems-oriented competitors such as ReDrafter, SpecInfer, ProPD, MagicDec, and optimized draft-model baselines are discussed but not evaluated under matched conditions.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a Findings recommendation. No code or artifact is identified, and essential details are missing: datastore sizes and preprocessing, exact calibration and grid-search procedures, calibration/evaluation separation, selected discount parameters, candidate-tree configurations and speculation lengths by setting, prompt sampling, random seeds, kernel modifications, and sufficient details of the customized vLLM/Ascend implementation.

The serving evaluation is methodologically under-specified. It uses only 100 prompts per context regime, provides no repeated trials, variance, confidence intervals, or significance analysis, and does not report standard serving metrics such as TTFT, inter-token latency, per-request latency distributions, or goodput under controlled arrival rates. Defining average latency as batch size divided by throughput is not generally equivalent to measuring request latency in continuous batching, especially with variable sequence lengths, and makes the latency-throughput claims difficult to validate.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess because REST and PIA are reimplemented and modified by the authors, while only PIA receives an end-to-end comparison. There are no ablations isolating the claimed benefits of interval sampling, shorter-prefix aggregation, calibration, OpenMP parallelization, and system/kernel optimizations in terms of final throughput.

The theoretical treatment is informative but simplified and only partially validated. It omits several real serving costs, assumes simplified attention dimensions, and extrapolates from an operator study on Llama2-7B and one accelerator. Consequently, it does not establish that hardware specifications alone reliably determine the speculation budget across architectures and platforms.

Some experimental choices introduce possible leakage or tuning bias: the paper says probability estimates are calibrated on generated text but does not specify which data are used or whether evaluation prompts are excluded. The construction and licensing/provenance implications of the ShareGPT-derived datastore are also insufficiently documented.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem: accelerating LLM serving under continuous batching, where many speculative-decoding methods lose their advantage.

The proposed combination of prompt/self-output retrieval with a fixed external datastore is sensible. The source-fusion mechanism and CPU-parallel retrieval implementation appear to improve candidate acceptance while avoiding a separately trained draft model.

The roofline discussion usefully connects batch size, speculation length, context length, attention cost, and matrix-multiplication efficiency. This provides intuition for why long-context workloads can retain a substantial speculation budget.

Experiments cover two model families, several tasks and context lengths, and batch sizes up to 64. On the reported Huawei Ascend setup, the end-to-end speedups over the authors' autoregressive baseline are substantial and consistent.
The method is parameter-free and its drafting stage runs on the host, which could make deployment simpler than approaches requiring auxiliary models or architectural modifications.
weaknesses: The central serving claims are substantially broader than the evidence. Statements such as being effective in “all use cases,” achieving state-of-the-art continuous-batching results, and outperforming autoregressive decoding at any latency constraint are supported only on one accelerator type, two similarly sized models, a customized serving stack, and a small collection of workloads.

The empirical comparison is inadequate for the claimed state of the art. End-to-end experiments primarily compare against autoregressive decoding and PIA; competitive large-batch methods discussed in the paper, such as ReDrafter, SpecInfer, ProPD, MagicDec, and optimized draft-model approaches, are not evaluated. Figure 4 compares REST and PIA mainly on acceptance and retrieval time, not full serving performance.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper does not provide code or sufficiently specify the customized vLLM system, kernel changes, datastore size and construction, memory footprint, sampling procedure, candidate-tree parameters, prefix thresholds, source-discount and calibration functions, grid-search space, speculation schedules by batch/context, CPU resource allocation, or exact experimental prompts and subsets.

The continuous-batching evaluation does not resemble a realistic serving study. Requests appear to be submitted whenever capacity is available, but there is no controlled arrival process, request-rate sweep, SLO/goodput analysis, or reporting of TTFT and TBT distributions. The paper instead defines “average latency” as batch size divided by throughput, which is a per-token proxy rather than measured per-request latency and can obscure variation in output lengths and scheduling behavior.

Reported results use only three subsets of 100 prompts, with unclear sampling and stopping details, and provide no repeated trials, uncertainty estimates, or error bars. It is therefore difficult to determine whether smaller differences are robust or whether system noise and workload composition influence the conclusions.

The cost comparison omits important resources introduced by SSSD: CPU cores, host memory, datastore construction/storage, and host-device coordination. Consequently, claims such as requiring four times less hardware or halving cost are not established by the reported accelerator throughput alone.

The theoretical analysis is largely an idealized operation-count argument. It assumes favorable weight reuse and hardware utilization, omits several system and kernel effects, and does not quantitatively validate its predicted optimal speculation budgets against the actual optimized serving implementation. Measurements of explicitly unoptimized operators do not substantiate conclusions about the customized optimized system.

Several conclusions overreach the presented ablations. Figure 4 shows aggregate accepted-token curves but does not establish that the fusion rule is optimal, nor does the paper compare against simple fusion alternatives or report sensitivity to its tuned discount/calibration parameters and datastore composition.

Generality remains uncertain: evaluation is restricted to 7B–8B dense Llama models, predominantly English datasets, and one hardware platform. There is no evidence for larger models, tensor-parallel or multi-device deployments, MoE models, other languages, or the disaggregated serving settings that motivate parts of the discussion.

The treatment of non-greedy decoding is incomplete. Only acceptance-rate changes are summarized, without end-to-end results or a precise account and validation of distributional equivalence. This weakens the claim that nearly equivalent results extend to nucleus sampling.

Overall, the idea is promising and the reported results justify further investigation, but missing implementation details, weak competitive evaluation, and nonstandard serving metrics prevent establishing a sound and reproducible Findings-level contribution in the current version. A next-cycle revision could plausibly address these issues.

strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/459b34d2672943d4929ac1b3bc0a6b65/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses the important practical problem of accelerating LLM serving under continuous batching, rather than evaluating speculative decoding only at batch size one.
The parameter-free design is appealing: it combines prompt/self-output lookup with an offline datastore, runs drafting on CPUs, and avoids training or deploying another model.

The roofline analysis usefully explains how batch size, speculation length, and context length affect different transformer operations. This systems perspective is relevant and generally clearly presented.

Experiments include two model/tokenizer configurations, several tasks, three context-length regimes, batch sizes up to 64, and end-to-end measurements including prefill. The reported 1.37–1.80x speedups at batch size 64 are promising.

The component and baseline comparisons support the narrower claim that prompt-derived and datastore-derived candidates are complementary and that SSSD offers a favorable acceptance-rate/retrieval-cost tradeoff against the evaluated parameter-free methods.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is presently inadequate for Findings. No code or artifact is provided, while crucial details are omitted: datastore size and memory footprint, preprocessing and tokenization, calibration data and learned discount parameters, grid-search ranges, speculation-length selection, exact serving-system modifications, operator implementations, and complete runtime settings.

The strongest claims are substantially broader than the evidence. Statements such as “effective in all use cases,” “any task,” and better throughput at “any latency requirement” are supported only by English datasets, two closely related 7–8B Llama models, and one Huawei accelerator.

The headline 4x result compares different operating points—SSSD at batch size 32 against autoregressive decoding at batch size 8—rather than measuring a 4x method-over-baseline gain under matched batching. Its interpretation also depends on defining latency as batch size divided by throughput instead of reporting directly measured per-request latency, TTFT, TBT, and tail percentiles.

The hardware evidence is narrow. The paper discusses NVIDIA behavior and distributed/disaggregated deployment but provides no experiments on NVIDIA GPUs, multiple accelerators, distributed inference, or production request-arrival traces. This limits validation of the claimed scalability and generality.

End-to-end comparisons against the broader state of the art are insufficient. REST is compared only through acceptance and retrieval measurements, PIA appears end-to-end only in one setting, and trained methods such as EAGLE/ReDrafter or long-context systems such as MagicDec are not benchmarked. Consequently, the “state-of-the-art” claim is not established.

The evaluation uses only 80–100 prompts per subset and reports no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analysis for datastore composition and calibration. Potential overlap between the conversational datastore and evaluation prompts is also not audited, although lookup-based acceleration is particularly sensitive to such overlap.

The theoretical analysis characterizes a potential near-free speculation budget under ideal roofline utilization, but the actual kernels remain imperfect and insufficiently documented. The connection between the idealized predictions and the end-to-end implementation is therefore suggestive rather than conclusively validated.

Overall, the core idea appears plausible and the results are encouraging, but missing reproducibility details and overgeneralized empirical claims prevent a clear Findings recommendation. A next-cycle revision with released implementation details, direct latency measurements, broader hardware/model evaluation, and stronger end-to-end baselines could become publishable.

strengths: The paper presents a practically relevant, training-free speculative-decoding system that combines prompt/self-output matching, an external suffix-array datastore, tree-based candidate fusion, and hardware-aware speculation. The complete manuscript was reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/694c956353dd4471a5b5e5a5c49feba8/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: 8B, 14B, and 70B models; conversational, mathematical, coding, agentic, multilingual, and long-context workloads; greedy and stochastic generation; multiple batch sizes; and both single-device and disaggregated serving configurations.

The reported results are compelling. SSSD consistently improves over autoregressive decoding and other retrieval-based methods, remains effective at larger batch sizes, and is competitive with or better than trained EAGLE variants in several shifted, reasoning, and long-context settings. The cold-start experiments are especially useful evidence for deployability.

The component analysis supports the claim that prompt/self-output candidates and datastore candidates are complementary. Comparing retrieval latency as well as acceptance length appropriately recognizes that speculative quality alone does not determine end-to-end performance.

The roofline discussion provides a useful systems perspective on how batch size, context length, grouped-query attention, and speculation length interact. The appendix supplies pseudocode and a reasonably detailed derivation rather than treating the hardware rule as an unexplained heuristic.
The paper is clearly written, visually polished, relevant to NLP infrastructure, and appropriately acknowledges limitations involving MoE/MLA models, CPU resources, and privacy.
weaknesses: The strongest production-serving claims are not fully supported by the evaluation. Most short-context experiments use offline fixed batches, and “latency” is defined as batch size divided by aggregate throughput rather than measured per-request latency under continuous batching and varying arrival rates. There is no comparison of goodput, tail latency, or saturation behavior in a realistic online workload.

Datastore construction is insufficiently controlled and documented. The paper uses model-family generations, translated ShareGPT/Synthia samples, The Stack, and reasoning traces chosen to benefit particular evaluated domains, but does not give exact dataset versions, mixture sizes, filtering, or deduplication against evaluation prompts and answers. This weakens the claims of task-independent deployment and robustness, even though exact verification should preserve output quality.

Baseline fairness is uncertain. SSSD receives a hardware-derived speculation budget and a warm, heterogeneous datastore, whereas EAGLE and Lookahead mainly use SGLang defaults; Lookahead is cold in the main end-to-end evaluation. The statement that alternative tuning gave limited benefit is not backed by sweeps. A comparison under matched tuning budgets and warm-start information would be needed for strong state-of-the-art claims.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the statement that code is provided. The manuscript lacks an artifact location, exact SGLang and implementation revisions, complete datastore recipes, CPU specifications, host-memory use, preprocessing/build costs, tuning-grid details, seeds, and several dataset-generation parameters. Some appendix pseudocode is explicitly not the implementation and appears ambiguous in its iterative prefix slicing and stopping conditions.

The hardware-aware rule is motivated theoretically but not directly validated against exhaustive or oracle speculation-length choices, fixed-length controls, or a broad hardware sweep. The cap at small batch sizes remains heuristic, and tensor-parallel communication is omitted from the model despite being relevant to the 70B experiments.

For nonzero-temperature decoding, the paper relies on a “simplified” SGLang speculative-sampling procedure and asserts exact preservation of the target distribution, but does not specify the verifier sufficiently or provide an empirical equivalence test. Because losslessness is central to speculative decoding, this deserves a precise algorithm or validation.

Uncertainty reporting is weak: only selected experiments state that five runs were averaged, plots lack error bars, and many results are available only as dense curves rather than numerical tables. The multilingual study also covers only a few languages and translated MT-Bench prompts, so claims concerning lower-resource-language robustness should be narrowed.

The method stores prior user/model interactions, yet the evaluation does not quantify update overhead, datastore eviction behavior, concurrent-query CPU scaling, multi-replica synchronization, or privacy-preserving per-user datastore performance. These omissions matter because low operational complexity is a central claimed advantage.

Overall, the work appears sound enough for Findings and is close to a main-conference recommendation. Confidence in the stronger recommendation is limited chiefly by the mismatch between the broad production claims and the offline evaluation, incomplete datastore controls, and uncertain baseline tuning rather than by a demonstrated failure of the core method.

strengths: SSSD is a practically motivated combination of prompt/self-output matching, suffix-array retrieval, candidate-tree fusion, and hardware-aware speculation. Avoiding an auxiliary neural drafter is operationally valuable, and exact verification preserves the target model's output distribution.

The evaluation is broader than is typical for speculative-decoding work: it covers several model sizes and families, greedy and sampled decoding, multiple tasks and languages, long-context and disaggregated-serving settings, and batch-size-dependent latency-throughput behavior.

The comparisons include strong trained methods and several parameter-free baselines. Using the same datastore for SSSD and REST is a useful control, while the source ablation and cold-start experiments help explain where gains arise.
The paper is generally clear, and the roofline discussion provides useful intuition about how batch size, context length, and speculation length interact.
weaknesses: The evidence is not sufficiently reproducible. The exact datastore contents, dataset proportions, preprocessing, grid-search space, selected fusion parameters, CPU and host-memory configuration, software versions, and many workload details are absent. The appendix explicitly says its algorithms are not exact replicas of the implementation and omits construction of key data structures; the manuscript asserts that code is provided but gives no accessible artifact reference.

Baseline fairness is unresolved. SSSD receives method-specific hardware-aware parameters and curated datastores, whereas EAGLE and Lookahead use SGLang defaults; the authors acknowledge that exhaustive baseline tuning was not performed. Lookahead is also evaluated cold in the end-to-end experiments despite warm-cache results being reported elsewhere. Consequently, the claimed parity or superiority over leading approaches cannot be cleanly attributed to SSSD itself.

Several datastores are tailored to evaluated workloads: The Stack is added for code, German translations for the German benchmark, and same-family reasoning traces for MATH. These are legitimate deployment choices, but they weaken claims of task-independent adoption, robustness under distribution shift, and absence of data preparation. No controlled comparison quantifies the benefit from this benchmark-aligned curation.

The production-serving claims exceed the evaluated setup. Most experiments use offline batches with all prompts available initially, and latency is derived as batch size divided by throughput rather than measured under continuous batching with request arrivals, queueing, and service-level objectives. The disaggregated experiments deliberately overprovision prefill. CPU utilization, contention, datastore-update cost, memory footprint beyond one 13 GB example, and total system cost are not reported.

The proposed hardware-selection rule is only a coarse roofline heuristic with ad hoc caps, ignores communication and kernel inefficiency, and is not validated against an exhaustive optimum across hardware, models, batch sizes, and context lengths. Thus the claim that it dynamically selects a near-optimal speculation length remains insufficiently supported.

Uncertainty reporting is weak: most plots lack error bars or confidence intervals, run counts are not consistently stated, and there are no statistical tests. Some conclusions rely on modest differences between methods, so run-to-run variability could affect them.

The contribution appears incremental relative to REST, prompt lookup, and Lookahead: its merit is chiefly in combining known retrieval sources and engineering them effectively. That could still support Findings if soundly documented, but the present reproducibility, comparison, and resource-accounting gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation. These issues seem addressable within a review cycle, motivating a borderline score rather than rejection of the underlying idea.

strengths: The paper presents a practically meaningful systems contribution: SSSD combines prompt/self-output matching, a continuously updateable suffix-array datastore, tree-based verification, and hardware-aware speculation without training or deploying an auxiliary model. The method is technically plausible and clearly motivated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/54ad9c3294c346a9a24403a52fcaf39c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation is unusually broad for a speculative-decoding paper, covering multiple model scales and families, batch sizes, languages, task domains, stochastic reasoning generation, long contexts, and both single-device and disaggregated serving settings.

End-to-end latency-throughput measurements in SGLang are more persuasive than acceptance-rate-only evaluation. Comparisons include strong trained methods such as EAGLE-3, standard speculative decoding, and several parameter-free alternatives; SSSD consistently improves over autoregressive decoding and is especially competitive under domain/language shift and long contexts.

The component analysis supports the central design intuition that prompt/self-output candidates and datastore candidates are complementary. Cold-start experiments also provide useful evidence that the system can deliver immediate, then progressively improving, acceleration.

The paper is clearly organized, provides helpful pseudocode and a roofline analysis, acknowledges unfavorable MoE/MLA regimes and CPU-memory requirements, and discusses privacy implications of retaining previous outputs.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet fully convincing from the manuscript. It says code is provided but gives no identifiable repository or artifact reference, describes the pseudocode as only logically equivalent to the implementation, and does not precisely enumerate all datastore datasets, preprocessing procedures, datastore mixtures, grid-search ranges, final hyperparameters, or per-benchmark sample sizes.

Baseline fairness limits the strength of the headline comparisons. SSSD receives method-specific parameter selection and task-relevant datastore content, including code and translated data, whereas EAGLE and Lookahead mostly use SGLang defaults; the authors acknowledge that exhaustive baseline tuning was not performed. The main Lookahead evaluation is cold because warm-starting is unsupported, although warm results in the smaller analysis indicate that initialization can matter.

Uncertainty reporting is weak. Some experiments are averaged over five runs, but most latency-throughput plots show no error bars, confidence intervals, or run-to-run variation. The paper also lacks a systematic statistical comparison at matched latency or throughput, making small claimed advantages difficult to assess.

The hardware-aware rule is appealing but is validated on a narrow set of accelerator configurations and is not directly compared against an exhaustive per-setting optimum. It ignores communication costs under tensor parallelism and uses caps and implementation-dependent qualifications, so the broader claim of near-optimal automatic speculation-length selection is stronger than the evidence.

Several deployment costs are incompletely quantified: CPU utilization, host-memory footprint as the datastore grows, suffix-array update/rebuild cost, and concurrent-request contention are not reported. The 13 GB datastore used for the 70B experiments also tempers the characterization of the method as uniformly lightweight.

Overall, the work appears sound and potentially valuable, but these reproducibility, baseline-control, and systems-measurement gaps prevent a confident main-conference recommendation. It is stronger than a routine Findings contribution, hence a borderline-conference score.
